list.listitem: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare and potentially fatal reaction to a neuroleptic or antipsychotic drug, or to the withdrawal of a patient from dopaminergic medication. C
Patients typically present with fever, altered mental status, muscle rigidity, fluctuating blood pressure and autonomic instability. C
Likelihood of NMS is greater within the first 14 days of therapy, if prior history of NMS, severe agitation, dehydration, physical restraints, or high environmental temperature. B
Immediate management is to discontinue neuroleptic and provide aggressive supportive therapy. C
Bromocriptine (enterally) and dantrolene (IV) may shorten the duration of NMS. C

background.definition: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare and potentially fatal idiosyncratic reaction to a neuroleptic or antipsychotic drug, or to the withdrawal of a patient from dopaminergic medication. Fever, altered mental status, muscle rigidity, fluctuating blood pressure and autonomic instability are defining symptoms.

list.listitem: Incidence of NMS has declined in recent years and is now estimated to be 0.1 to 0.2 new cases per 1000 persons per year.
Approximately 2000 cases of NMS are diagnosed annually in the U.S.
In one series of 223 psychiatric inpatients, 2.2% had NMS with their first exposure to an antipsychotic.
NMS appears to be more common in men than women (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.2-1.8) and peaks in incidence at age 20 to 25 years.
Rapid escalation or administration of large doses of neuroleptic medication over a short interval to a confused and often volume contracted patient presenting with severe psychomotor agitation.
NMS may develop in a patient on maintanence neuroleptic doses after several years of use. The symptom presentation covers a spectrum, and no there is no correlation with drug potency, age or sex.
NMS may also occur in Parkinson's patients in whom dopaminergic medications are withdrawn and in patients taking metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, clotiapine, or tricyclic antidepressants.

Cases of NMS caused by second generation antipsychotics have been reported. A systematic review identified 6 primary studies which concluded that the incidence was lower and NMS was less severe with 2nd generation neuroleptics, but that it does occur, as evidenced by identification of 186 case reports.

All classes of neuroleptics or drugs producing dopamine D2-receptor blockage may cause NMS. Blockage of dopamine receptors in the hypothalamus and corpus striatum is postulated to disrupt control of the sympathetic nervous system resulting in autonomic dysregulation and muscle rigidity.
NMS can also be caused by relative dopamine deficits induced by abrupt discontinuation of a dopamine agonist (eg, amantidine or levodopa).

A systematic review identified 9 RCTs with 1648 patients that compared diphenhydramine with placebo or another agent for prevention of neuroleptic adverse effects. There was no effect on akathisia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, restlessness, or sedation. A subgroup analysis of the 4 placebo controlled trials did find a reduction in extrapyramidal adverse events (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41-0.90). B
Typical presentation is fever, rigidity, and mental status decline in a patient receiving neuroleptic medication. C
Elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and leukocytosis are common. C

Differential.Differential_Features: May appear identical to NMS symptoms
Similar symptoms without neuroleptic, but includes more GI symptoms
History or diagnosis associated with dopaminaergic use
Absence of ridgidity and history substance abuse
Hot, dry skin, absence of sweating

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: The International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for neuroleptic malignant syndrome have good accuracy in comparison with modified DSM-IV-TR criteria, using a cutoff score of 74 points. The criteria include: (1) exposure to a dopamine agonist, or dopamine agonist withdrawal, within the past 72 hours, (2) hyperthermia, (3) rigidity, (4) mental status alteration, (5) elevated creatine phosphokinase, (6) sympathetic nervous system lability (2 or more of elevated BP, BP fluctuation [≥25 mm Hg systolic or ≥20 mm Hg diastolic within 24 hours], diaphoresis, or urinary incontinence), (7) tachycardia and tachypnea, and (8) negative work-up for infectious, toxic, metabolic, and neurologic causes.

list.listitem: Suspect NMS in a profusely diaphoretic patient with hyperthermia, unstable blood pressure, muscle ridgidity, altered mental status, tachycardia, tachypnea, and dysphagia with sialorrhea occuring within 1 to 4 weeks of initiation of neuroleptic therapy.
Likewise, similar symptoms in a Parkinson's patient who has suddenly ceased use of levodopa or amantidine should suggest the diagnosis.

Patients with NMS caused by second generation antipsychotic drugs tend to be younger, are less likely to present with rigidity or extrapyramidal signs (compared to those with NMS induced by use of a first generation antipsychotic).
Be sure to consider serotonin syndrome in the differential diagnosis.

No specific laboratory studies are diagnostic. Most patients will have significant increases in CPK (>1000 U/L), aldolase, transaminases, and lactic acid related to rhabdomyolysis. Leukocytosis (12-30,000), azotemia, and hypoxia are often present.
Initial evaluation should include CPK, aldolase, tramsaminases, lactic acid, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, Ca, Mg, CBC, blood culture, TSH, urine myoglobin, and coagulation studies.
Blood cultures, CSF analysis, and neuroimaging studies are usually negative or normal in NMS but should be part of the evaluation for altered mental status if the diagnosis is not clear.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Discontinue the causative drug, treat fever aggressively, and provide intensive supportive care. C

Dantrolene and bromocriptene are widely used but evidence of effectiveness is lacking; there is a suggestion from a review of case reports that dantrolene use is associated with increased mortality. C
Bromocriptine (enterally) and dantrolene (IV) are traditionally used to shorten the duration of NMS, but there have been no clinical trials.
A case report and review of case reports concluded that bromocriptine may be effective for reversing persistent residual catatonia following NMS.

A systematic review of case reports identified 187 cases in the literature that reported the type of therapy. None were randomized or controlled clinical trials. Dantrolene monotherapy (n = 30) was associated with more rapid improvement within 24 hours (77% vs 23% for those not receiving it) but also a 16% mortality rate. Patients receiving only supportive therapy had a slower initial response but a similar overall duration of symptoms to those treated with dantrolene, and a lower mortality (2.0%). These conclusions are limited greatly by the very poor quality of the underlying evidence, selection bias, and other issues.
Outcomes do not seem to be worse for long-acting injectable versus oral antipsychotics based on a systematic review of 662 case reports.
Continue dopamine agonists if currently used.

Methyprednisolone pulse therapy (methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3 days) was studied in a small RCT with 40 Parkinson's patients. Median duration of symptoms was 7 days in the steroid group and 18 days in the placebo group (statistical significance not reported). All patients also received levodopa, bromocriptine, and dantrolene.
Amantadine and benzodiazepines have also been proposed in case reports but clinical trials are lacking.
Immediately discontinue the neuroleptic drug.
Management should include control of fever with antipyretics and physical cooling, along with correction of fluid and electrolytes disturbances.
Continued monitoring of vital signs, maintanence of kidney function, DVT prophylaxis and nutritional support are thought to improve outcomes but clinical trials are largely lacking.
For patients who do not respond to supportive and/or drug therapy, electroconvulsive therapy has been proposed in case reports.
Complications include rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravscular coagulation, and acute renal failure.
Consider alkalinization of fluids if a patient has significant rhabdomyolysis.
Mortality rate is 10%. Prognosis depends on prompt recognition, immediate drug discontinuation, and aggressive and intensive medical care. B

A systematic review of 683 case reports and case series (median age 36, 62% male) found that continued use of antipsychotics (OR 4.4), respiratory problems (OR 3.5), greater severity of hyperthermia (OR 1.3) and older age (OR 1.05 per year) were associated with higher mortality. There was no association with antipsychotic class. B
Outcomes do not seem to be worse for long-acting injectable versus oral antipsychotics based on a systematic review of 662 case reports. B
Route of drug administration affects the symptom duration. Average is 2 weeks for oral and 4 weeks for intramuscular drug routes. B
Most mortality attributable to kidney failure or aspiration pneumonia; cardiac complications and DIC also contribute. B

algorithm.title: Suggested Approach to the Patient with Suspected Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS).

cell.label: NMS suspected: fever, altered mental status, muscle rigidity, diaphoresis, tremor, and/or unstable vitals in patient at risk (history of psychosis or Parkinson's, neuroleptic or dopamine agonist use)?
Discontinue neuroleptic and order CPK, aldolase, CBC, electrolytes, BUN, serum creatinine, TSH, calcium, magnesium, and blood cultures. NMS likely (elevated CK, no other diagnoses likely)?
Consider other diagnoses, e.g., sepsis, infection, other drug reaction, thyrotoxicosis, delirium tremens, CNS disease.
Intensive monitoring, fever reduction, correct electrolyte disturbances, aggressive isotonic IV fluids to prevent kidney failure from myoglobinuria.
Consider pharmacotherapy with bromocriptine or dantrolene and resume dopamine agonist if prior use.
